articles.title: Scientists recreate a bizarre quantum effect that stops a particle cold

paras.en: Scientists recreate a bizarre quantum effect that stops a particle cold

- Oxford physicists have recreated a bizarre quantum effect in which a particle responds to a magnetic field without ever traveling through it. Using a hybrid quantum computer, they demonstrated how introducing a simulated magnetic flux could completely halt a particle's movement through quantum interference. The experiment brings a decades-old prediction into a new setting where matter and quantum fields influence one another.

A particle does not have to pass through a magnetic field to be influenced by it. That surprising feature of quantum physics has now been recreated by researchers at the University of Oxford, who used a hybrid quantum computer to demonstrate how an invisible magnetic influence can bring a simulated particle's movement to a complete stop.

The experiment reproduced a phenomenon known as the Aharonov-Bohm effect, in which a charged particle traveling around a region containing magnetic flux experiences a measurable change in its quantum state, even though its path never takes it through the magnetic field itself.

The Oxford team achieved this using a quantum system that combines qubits, the basic units of quantum information, with quantum oscillators, which represent vibrating motion. Their findings, published in Nature Physics, demonstrate how this combination could help scientists investigate fundamental interactions between matter and fields that are increasingly difficult to simulate using conventional computers.
A Strange Quantum Effect Predicted in 1959

In everyday physics, a charged particle responds to the electric and magnetic fields it encounters. Quantum mechanics, however, reveals that particles can behave in ways that have no straightforward counterpart in our ordinary experience.

In 1959, physicists Yakir Aharonov and David Bohm predicted that a charged particle could be affected by magnetic flux even if it traveled entirely outside the region containing the magnetic field. Rather than experiencing a conventional magnetic force along its path, the particle would undergo a change in its quantum phase.

Quantum phase describes an aspect of a particle's wave behavior that influences how different possible paths interfere with one another. Although the phase itself is not directly visible, differences in phase can produce measurable effects.

The prediction became known as the Aharonov-Bohm effect and was eventually verified in experiments involving real electrons. It remains one of the clearest demonstrations that the quantum world operates according to rules that go beyond the familiar laws of classical physics.
Researchers are now exploring how this phenomenon behaves in more complex theoretical systems known as lattice gauge theories.

These theories describe how matter interacts with fields associated with fundamental forces. They represent space as a grid, with matter located at individual points and fields associated with the connections between them. Such models are particularly important in particle physics and high-energy physics, where scientists study the basic particles and interactions that make up the universe.

The challenge is that the mathematics becomes extraordinarily demanding as these systems grow more complicated. Even powerful conventional computers can struggle to calculate how all the interacting components evolve.

Quantum computers offer a different approach. Instead of attempting to calculate every aspect of a quantum system using classical computing methods, scientists can construct another quantum system that follows the same underlying rules. They can then observe its behavior directly, an approach known as quantum simulation.
How Scientists Built the Quantum Experiment

The Oxford project began in 2022, when lead author Dr. Sebastian Saner, Dr. Oana Bazavan, and their colleagues started developing a way to simulate lattice gauge theories using a hybrid quantum system. They collaborated with Dr. Alejandro Bermudez of the Instituto de Física Teórica in Madrid.
Their experimental design relied on two different quantum components that performed separate functions.

The first consisted of qubits encoded in the internal states of trapped ions, which are electrically charged atoms held in place using electromagnetic fields. These qubits represented the gauge fields in the theoretical model.
The second component used quantum oscillators, created by the vibrations of those same trapped ions. These oscillators represented matter.

By combining the two, the researchers constructed a simple loop that served as a basic building block of a lattice gauge theory. Two oscillators represented matter at two different locations, while two qubits represented the fields connecting those locations.
Although the arrangement was small, it was sufficient to reproduce an important interaction between matter and magnetic flux.
Quantum Entanglement Creates a Surprising Solution

The researchers next placed the two qubits into an entangled quantum state. Entanglement is a phenomenon in which quantum systems become linked in ways that cannot be fully explained by classical physics.
Within the team's simulated lattice gauge theory, this entangled state represented magnetic flux passing through the center of the loop.

Initially, the researchers had planned to introduce the magnetic flux as a fixed background condition. However, creating the necessary interaction would have required capabilities that their quantum hardware did not possess.

Encoding the flux directly into the qubits provided a practical alternative. More importantly, it allowed the magnetic flux to become part of the evolving quantum system rather than remaining an unchanging external influence.

"For us, the exciting step was to encode the magnetic flux in a gauge field that was itself dynamical," says Dr. Saner. "Rather than having matter evolve in a fixed background, the matter and gauge field become part of the same quantum dynamics."

What began as a technical workaround ultimately enabled the researchers to explore a more interesting version of the phenomenon, one in which matter and the field could participate together in the quantum dynamics.
A Quantum Effect That Stops Particle Motion
With their simulated loop in place, the scientists examined how a matter particle moved between locations through a process known as quantum tunneling.
Quantum tunneling allows particles to move between states in ways that would not be possible under ordinary classical rules.
When the researchers ran their simulation without magnetic flux, the particle could tunnel freely around the loop.
Introducing the simulated flux produced a strikingly different result.

The particle had two possible paths around the loop, but the magnetic flux changed their relative quantum phases. As a result, the two paths interfered destructively, meaning their quantum contributions canceled each other out.
This interference completely suppressed the tunneling, leaving the simulated particle frozen in its original state.

The outcome demonstrated the Aharonov-Bohm effect within a lattice gauge theory containing a dynamical field. Rather than simply reproducing the familiar behavior of a particle moving around a fixed magnetic influence, the experiment showed how the phenomenon can emerge when matter and the field are both represented by interacting quantum components.
A New Tool for Exploring Fundamental Physics
The Oxford findings were published alongside a related study by researchers at the University of Maryland, led by Professor Norbert Linke.

The Maryland team also used a hybrid quantum system, but their experiment focused on simulating the Yukawa potential, a mathematical description of an interaction relevant to nuclear and particle physics.
Although the two research groups developed their methods independently, they later coordinated the submission of their studies to Nature Physics.
Together, the experiments demonstrate how hybrid quantum computers could become valuable tools for investigating fundamental interactions that are difficult to reproduce using classical simulations.
By combining different types of quantum components, researchers can build systems in which matter and fields are represented in ways that more closely reflect the physics they want to study.

The Oxford experiment provides an example of that potential. A phenomenon first predicted in 1959 and later observed with electrons has now been recreated in a quantum simulator where the field itself participates in the dynamics, offering scientists another way to explore the unusual rules governing the quantum world.

articles.title: DNA recording system reveals how a single cell becomes a body

paras.en: DNA recording system reveals how a single cell becomes a body
Scientists have recorded how a single fertilized egg becomes a complex body, uncovering hidden patterns of development that could shed light on birth defects and cancer.
- University of Washington School of Medicine/UW Medicine

- Scientists have traced the development of a mouse embryo from its first two cells to the formation of organs, using a remarkable DNA recording system that reveals the family history of individual cells. Their findings uncover how different cell types emerge on their own schedules and could help explain what goes wrong in birth defects, genetic disorders, and cancer.

Scientists have reconstructed a remarkably detailed family tree of cells in a developing mouse embryo, tracing their origins back to the moment a fertilized egg first divided into two cells. Using an innovative DNA recording technology, the researchers followed how those early cells multiplied, developed specialized roles, and eventually helped form a body with distinct organs and tissues.
The recording covered the first 13.5 days of embryonic development, providing an unusually detailed look at how a complex mammalian body takes shape. (Full gestation in mice is 19 to 21 days.)
The findings, published on October 8, 2026, in the journal Science, could help scientists better understand normal development and what happens when that process goes wrong.

"We are interested in tracking how cells' early ancestry in an embryo influences their later fates. Exploring cell lineages helps decode normal development. Such research could eventually advance knowledge about congenital malformations, neurodevelopmental conditions, genetic disorders or cancer," said Dr. Jay Shendure, a professor of genome sciences at the University of Washington School of Medicine in Seattle and a Howard Hughes Medical Institute Investigator.
Shendure led the research alongside Dr. Chengxiang Qiu, a molecular and systems biologist at Dartmouth College in New Hampshire. Both served as senior authors of the study.
A DNA Typewriter Records the History of Living Cells
The achievement was made possible by a technology called DNA Typewriter, developed by Shendure and Junhong Choi, who is now at Sloan Kettering Cancer Center.
Rather than simply observing cells as they divide, the system allows scientists to preserve a record of their history directly within their DNA.

To accomplish this, the researchers inserted a redesigned recording sequence, which they call a tape, into the genome of a fertilized mouse egg. The updated design made it easier to recover the information stored in individual cells.

As the embryo developed, the DNA Typewriter remained embedded in the genetic material of its cells, recording their divisions in a way that could later be used to reconstruct their ancestry. The result was something like a biological logbook, documenting the sequence of events that gave rise to different cell populations.

"Think of it like an actual typewriter, except it types onto a cell's own DNA instead of paper," explained Haedong Kim, a co-first author of the study and a postdoctoral scientist in genome sciences at UW Medicine, the Seattle Hub for Synthetic Biology and the Howard Hughes Medical Institute. "Every time a cell divides, it strikes one new character onto the next blank line -- always in order, never overwriting what's already there. Because the characters are always filled in sequence, that sequence itself spells out the cell's division history."
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Because these markings are passed down to daughter cells, researchers can examine the recorded sequences and identify which cells descended from a shared ancestor. Cells carrying matching portions of the record can be linked together, allowing scientists to reconstruct branches of the embryo's family tree.
"Writing the record is only half the problem. You also have to read it back out of each cell, so we redesigned the tape to make that easier," said Kim.
Overcoming a Major Challenge in Developmental Biology

Reconstructing the entire history of a developing mammal has long been a formidable challenge. As an embryo grows, its cells divide repeatedly and begin taking on specialized functions. Following those relationships becomes increasingly difficult as the number and variety of cells expand.
Scientists accomplished a similar feat decades ago in a tiny roundworm, but that animal has a relatively simple body with far fewer cells. Its transparency also makes development easier to study.

Mammals are considerably more complicated. Earlier technologies provided important insights into mouse embryonic development, but they generally captured only portions of the larger cellular family tree.

Some traditional recording techniques also have significant limitations. They work by cutting DNA to create identifying marks, which can damage cells and erase information left by earlier divisions. Their recording capacity is limited, and because the marks are not necessarily created in a fixed sequence, scientists must attempt to reconstruct the order of events afterward.

"DNA Typewriter avoids all of this," said Kim. "It writes without fully severing the DNA, keeps recording relatively steadily, and writes everything in strict order, so we can record cell lineages at much higher resolution for a longer time."
Tracing an Embryo Back to Its First Two Cells
The researchers began by attempting to record development in 100 fertilized mouse eggs. Of those, 10 embryos were ultimately available for examination.

One specimen, identified as Embryo No. 3, stood out because its DNA recording system had functioned particularly well and preserved the most extensive developmental history. The scientists therefore concentrated their detailed analysis on that embryo.
One of the most important discoveries came from a recording made at the very beginning of development, immediately after the fertilized egg divided for the first time.

"Our recording captured a clear, permanent mark distinguishing the two very first cells, letting us trace nearly every cell we profiled from the embryo back to one or the other," said Kim. "One of these two founding cells did go on to produce more descendants than the other, but they produced diverse cell types at almost equal ratios."
This meant that although one of the original cells contributed more descendants overall, both founding cells gave rise to a remarkably similar mix of specialized cell types.
The finding illustrates how scientists can now investigate the earliest stages of development with a level of detail that was previously difficult to achieve.
Scientists Discover When Cells Choose Their Roles
The DNA recordings also revealed important information about when cells begin committing to their eventual roles in the body.

Early embryonic cells can give rise to many different types of tissue. As development progresses, their descendants gradually become more specialized, eventually forming structures such as the nervous system, skin, blood, and eyes.
By reconstructing the branches of the embryo's cellular family tree, the researchers could determine when different groups of cells began following distinct developmental paths.
Their observations were consistent with conclusions drawn from decades of previous research, but the new approach allowed them to examine these patterns within a single developing mouse.

"Blood cells and the retina committed relatively early, while the skin's outer layer didn't commit until noticeably later," the researchers explained. "Cell fate wasn't locked in all at once. Different cell types settled into their identity on their own separate schedules, some early and some late."
These findings show that the transition from a flexible, unspecialized cell to one with a particular biological function does not happen at the same time throughout the embryo.

Instead, different tissues follow their own developmental timelines. Some cells begin narrowing their possible futures early, while others remain flexible for a longer period before becoming committed to a specific role.
What This Could Mean for Birth Defects, Cancer, and Stem Cell Therapies
Understanding exactly how cells acquire their identities could eventually have important implications for medicine.

Many developmental disorders arise when the normal process of cell specialization or tissue formation is disrupted. Cancer also involves abnormal cell behavior, including failures in the mechanisms that ordinarily regulate cell growth and division.
By tracing cellular ancestry and identifying when different developmental pathways emerge, scientists may gain a clearer understanding of how these problems begin.

"This kind of large-scale developmental recording gives scientists a map of how one cell becomes a whole body -- which helps explain how organs form correctly, how that process can go wrong in birth defects, and how abnormal cell growth drives cancer. As stem cell engineering advances, this kind of recording can also help guide how we engineer cells for therapeutic use."

Although the work was conducted in mouse embryos and does not yet represent a direct medical treatment, it demonstrates a powerful way to study the biological decisions that shape a developing organism.
The approach could also support future stem cell research, particularly efforts to guide cells toward specific identities for regenerative medicine and other therapeutic applications.

Additional co-first authors included Qi Yu and Sophie Seidel, both affiliated with the University of Washington School of Medicine's Department of Genome Sciences and the Seattle Hub for Synthetic Biology.

Shendure serves as the lead scientific director of the Seattle Hub for Synthetic Biology. He is also scientific director of the UW Medicine Brotman Baty Institute for Precision Medicine and the Allen Institute for Cell Lineage Tracing.

articles.title: 'We basically did Top Gun in space': 'Star Trek Starfleet Academy' warps back into action in March 2027 for sophomore year in the final frontier
articles.author: Tariq Malik

paras.en: NEW YORK — Set your phasers to back-to-school, space fans. Star Trek is going back to Starfleet Academy for season 2, and we finally have a release date.

The sophomore season of "Star Trek: Starfleet Academy" will warp back to the small screen in March 2027 when the limited series returns for its final season on Paramount+. The series, which follows a class of cadets balancing Starfleet classes, space adventures (and yes, some love) in the 32nd century, will return with its full cast and even add new faces, showrunners announced at a panel at New York Comic Con 2026 on Saturday (Oct. 10).

"Season one is about letting go of who you were in the past to start again at Starfleet Academy," executive producer and co-showrunner Noga Landau said in the Star Trek panel. "Season two is about thinking that you knew who you were, only to realize that as you grow older, your life is going to go in directions you didn't expect, and you're going to have to shift your perception of yourself. So it's really about sophomore year, right?"
Paramount+ with SHOWTIME (no ads): $11.99 /mo
Star Trek: Starfleet Academy will be available to watch on Paramount+. You can also watch almost every other Star Trek show and movie on there, too, while you wait.

Holly Hunter returns as academy chancellor Nahla Ake, a long-lived half-Lanthanite, who will have to face a familiar face in her estranged father, Nyk Ake, portrayed by Bill Nighy (Living, About Time) in season two.

"He plays my full lanthanide father, who has basically, if he wants, can achieve immortality," Hunter said, dropping a big preview about her character in season two. "He plays my dad, and I play me ... and my twin, my twin sister. Very fun."
Also joining this year's Starfleet Academy class is Rosemarie DeWitt (Untamed, The Staircase) as Laytha Sadal, the First Lady of Betazed (and mother of Academy cadet Tarima).

"We have had such a blast," Hunter said of working with the entire cast of Starfleet Academy. "It was a tremendous honor and learning experience for me to do the show for two seasons, and I just really am excited about the second season because there's so much more intimacy that we just comfortably felt with each other over those 10 episodes."

In season one, Starfleet Academy brought back Trek's favorite Emergency Medical Hologram, The Doctor (Robert Picardo), then gave the 800-year-old Star Trek: Voyager physician a daughter in the photonic Sam (Kerrice Brooks) and a Klingon medical student, Jay-Den Kraag (Karim Diané), to train.

"His future existence is forever changed. Nothing will ever be the same for the character," Picardo said in the panel. "The shock of that, and how that changed the character, [...] informs all of season two. My primary relationships are now with my daughter and of course with Jay-Den, as I'm mentoring him as a future physician, and we have some terrific scenes together as well."

Executive producer and co-showrunner Alex Kurtzman promised more space action in season two of Starfleet Academy and showed an exclusive teaser clip of Academy cadets Caleb (Sandro Rosta), Genesis (Bella Shepard) and Sam as they race to recover data from a crashed spaceship on their first away mission. But the best, Kurtzman said, is yet to come when the show's cadets meet up with Nova Squadron, the elite flight team at Starfleet Academy.

"The Nova Squadron episode is amazing on a lot of different levels," Kurtzman said. "We basically did Top Gun in space. "What's available to us now technologically allowed us to go to a place that I don't think we've ever gone to on television before. Certainly not in Star Trek."
Star Trek: Starfleet Academy will return to TV in March 2027 on the Paramount+ streaming platform.
Paramount+ with SHOWTIME (no ads): $11.99 /mo
Star Trek: Starfleet Academy will be available to watch on Paramount+. You can also watch almost every other Star Trek show and movie on there, too, while you wait.

Tariq is the award-winning Editor-in-Chief of Space.com and joined the team in 2001. He covers human spaceflight, as well as skywatching and entertainment. He became Space.com's Editor-in-Chief in 2019. Before joining Space.com, Tariq was a staff reporter for The Los Angeles Times covering education and city beats in La Habra, Fullerton and Huntington Beach. He's a recipient of the 2022 Harry Kolcum Award for excellence in space reporting and the 2025 Space Pioneer Award from the National Space Society. He is an Eagle Scout and Space Camp alum with journalism degrees from the USC and NYU. You can find Tariq at Space.com and as the co-host to the This Week In Space podcast on the TWiT network. To see his latest project, you can follow Tariq on Twitter @tariqjmalik.

articles.title: See the original Galileo shuttle from 'Star Trek' in its new home at the Original Series Set Tour in New York
articles.author: Jeff Spry

paras.en: Nostalgia is a hell of a thing, especially when it comes to sci-fi. For "Star Trek" fans wanting to mark the franchise's 60th anniversary this year, a geeky pilgrimage to upstate New York should be on the cards. Why? Because alongside the splendid autumnal colors, they can steer over to Ticonderoga to behold the newly installed Galileo shuttlecraft.

After a complete two-year restoration project in 2012 headed up by superfan and collector Adam Schneider, this iconic fictional spacecraft, seen by millions in seven episodes over three seasons of "Star Trek: The Original Series," was recently relocated from its former home at the Johnson Space Center Museum in Houston, Texas.

It's now on permanent loan to James Cawley and his Star Trek Original Series Set Tour in historic downtown Ticonderoga, New York, where it joins a family of painstakingly detailed sets based on the official "Star Trek" blueprints.

'Galileo is still the property of Space Center, and it was on display there since 2013," Schneider tells Space. "It went to USS Intrepid for the 50th anniversary of 'Star Trek,' displayed under the Enterprise Space Shuttle. You had the Enterprise with Enterprise's little shuttle Galileo adjacent, which was an extraordinary picture. It went back to Space Center, but it takes up an enormous amount of room, and they took it off display after 8 years."

It seemed a shame to have the shuttle out of sight, so Schneider got to work finding a new home for the shuttle. "Since I was on the board, I tried to figure out a place where it could be aimed", recounts Schneider. "The Star Trek Tour made the most sense, so I worked with Space Center to relocate it, and it arrived a couple of years ago."

Hoping to give the restored relic its own private docking bay due to its enormity, faithful fans raised hundreds of thousands of dollars via a Kickstarter campaign led by Brian Mix and David Harvey, and built a beautiful building addition for Galileo to be safely ensconced in.

"My wife Leslie and I had been tending over the Galileo for a number of years, and it's now successfully displayed there in New York for all to see," Schneider adds. "It's an extraordinary thing to see person if you have not. It's not the size of a chair, it’s the size of a bus. It looks gorgeous in its new space, and if you’re a space aficionado or Star Trek aficionado, that’s even more reason to get involved with this thing."

Opening weekend for the general public at Star Trek Tours to see the newest member of the museum was Sept. 18-20, 2026, and the Galileo was the star attraction. Branded Trekonderoga Weekend, the unveiling ceremony was attended by Assemblymen Dan Stec and Dan Simpson, and 'Trek' luminaries George Takei, Jonathan Frakes, and Brent Spiner.

"We're certainly thrilled that we were able to work with Adam and NASA to get it here permanently," Cawley tells Space. "Then to get it on display properly and share it with all the fans and make sure that it's on exhibit for many years to come. We’re just outside of the village of Lake George, so we’re part of the greater Lake George tourism region.

"You've seen it on television, and now you’re the caretaker of it. What an honor to be able to do that. It’s the simplicity of the Galileo that makes it so unique. It's Matt Jefferies' whole design ethic for the original series. Less is more. It catches your eye in a specific way. It has a blocky-type silhouette and actually it really complements the Enterprise because you really see the shape difference. Everything has that mid-century modern aesthetic. It's just timeless."

For Cawley, being custodian and host of the screen-used Galileo is like a dream. This 23-foot-long mock-up was part of the USS Enterprise's basic design and was rescued from demolition some 14 years ago when Schneider purchased it at a 2012 memorabilia auction for $61,000.

"We had a great rousing opening weekend with it, and business has been very steady into October with people asking about it. It's going to be a big cornerstone to the tour. I think people are becoming aware that it’s here and they’re making a pilgrimage to come because of it."

For more prices, hours, and more information on the Star Trek Original Series Set Tour in Ticonderoga, New York, visit them at https://startrektour.com or call 518-503-5497. You can also see the Galileo in action in Star Trek: The Original Series on Paramount+.

Jeff Spry is an award-winning screenwriter and veteran freelance journalist covering TV, movies, video games, books, and comics. His work has appeared at SYFY Wire, Inverse, Collider, Bleeding Cool and elsewhere. Jeff lives in beautiful Bend, Oregon amid the ponderosa pines, classic muscle cars, a crypt of collector horror comics, and two loyal English Setters.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 13, 1773: Astronomer Charles Messier discovers the Whirlpool Galaxy before we ever knew it was a galaxy
articles.author: Hanneke Weitering

paras.en: On Oct. 13, 1773, a French astronomer named Charles Messier discovered the "Whirlpool Galaxy," also known as Messier 51, or M51.

Charles Messier was scanning the sky for objects that could confuse comet hunters when he catalogued the galaxy as M51. However, Messier wasn't able to see the spiral structure, and he didn't identify it as a galaxy.

Seventy-two years later, another astronomer named William Parsons saw the whirlpool shape, but he thought it was a spiral nebula. Eventually, Edwin Hubble found out that M51 and other features like it were actually galaxies.

The Whirlpool Galaxy is located about 31 million light-years from Earth and just might be the textbook case of a spiral galaxy. But in 1773, it was just one of 51 (at the time of its discovery) of "comet-like 'objects to avoid'" in the night sky.

The Whirlpool Galaxy's designation as M51 marks it as the 51st non-comet object catalogued by Messier, who was the chief astronomer of the Marine Observatory in Paris dedicated to studying comets. According to a NASA account, Messier stumbled across his first non-comet object, M1 (also known as the Crab Nebula), while studying a comet in 1758. The objects looked like fuzzy blobs like comets, but didn't move like a comet. By 1773, at the time he first spotted M51, he had catalogued over four dozen such objects to help prevent astronomers from mistaking them for comets.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The Whirlpool Galaxy appears as a dazzling spiral in images by the Hubble Space Telescope, and has a magnitude of 8.4 on the brightness scale used by astronomers. That means it can be observed through a small telescope ("most easily during May," NASA says) in the constellation Venatici (the Hunting Dogs) in the northern sky, just below the handle of the Big Dipper star pattern.

Scientists suspsect the Whirpool Galaxy gets is striking spiral shape from a close interaction with its neighbor galaxy NGC 5195, which may have passed through M51's main disk about 500 million years ago, scientists with NASA's Spitzer Space Telescope have said.

"This gravitational tug of war may also have triggered an increased level of star formation in M51," they added in a statement. "The companion galaxy's pull would be inducing extra starbirth by compressing gas, jump-starting the process by which stars form."
Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube.

Hanneke Weitering is a multimedia journalist in the Pacific Northwest reporting on the future of aviation at FutureFlight.aero and Aviation International News and was previously the Editor for Spaceflight and Astronomy news here at Space.com. As an editor with over 10 years of experience in science journalism she has previously written for Scholastic Classroom Magazines, MedPage Today and The Joint Institute for Computational Sciences at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. After studying physics at the University of Tennessee in her hometown of Knoxville, she earned her graduate degree in Science, Health and Environmental Reporting (SHERP) from New York University. Hanneke joined the Space.com team in 2016 as a staff writer and producer, covering topics including spaceflight and astronomy. She currently lives in Seattle, home of the Space Needle, with her cat and two snakes. In her spare time, Hanneke enjoys exploring the Rocky Mountains, basking in nature and looking for dark skies to gaze at the cosmos.

His appointment, alongside the addition of Theo Squires as Director of Strategy & Corporate Development, strengthens Agile’s ability to execute its long-term growth strategy, support capital formation, and pursue strategic opportunities as the company continues to scale.

Agile is entering its next phase with growing opportunities across the commercial and national security space. As Agile expands its capabilities and production capacity, the company is also strengthening the financial and strategic foundation needed to support its long-term objectives.

“Agile has built significant momentum, and our next phase of growth requires the financial capability and oversight to match our technical expertise,” said Chris Pearson, CEO of Agile Space Industries. “Jonathan’s experience in aerospace, capital formation and corporate transformation, combined with Theo’s focus on strategy and corporate development, will help us evaluate new opportunities, make strategic investments and position Agile for sustainable, long-term growth.”
Jonathan Baliff Joins Board of Directors

He previously served as president and CEO of Bristow Group and held senior leadership positions at NRG Energy and Credit Suisse. articles.title: Resource competition intensifies with surge in megaconstellations
articles.author: Hope Hodge Seck

paras.en: Amazon wants more than 5,000 satellites in orbit. Blue Origin has proposed another 5,400. Chinese companies have filed plans encompassing vastly more. Elon Musk has talked about a constellation numbering 1 million.
There is one issue: building all of them.

The unprecedented rush to put satellites into low Earth orbit is colliding with shortages of specialized components and materials, suppliers struggling to keep up and competition from the booming artificial intelligence industry. The squeeze is forcing satellite companies to rethink designs, accept delays and confront a more fundamental question about the timelines for what’s possible.

Competition for scarce resources and supplies amid surging demand is forcing tradeoffs in industry that threaten to delay launches and may push companies out of the market or trigger greater consolidation.

“Companies right now are just looking at where they might be able to take additional risk,” said Steve Jordan Tomaszewski, vice president of space systems for the Aerospace Industries Association. He participated in a supply chain analysis with audit firm PricewaterhouseCoopers earlier this year that involved talking to dozens of industry representatives.

Tomaszewski said supply chain challenges have companies looking for “where they can maybe downgrade something to not using a space-qualified component … Maybe they’re okay waiting a year for a certain type of valve because they know that’s going to be something they really have to deliver on.”

The 54-page analysis isolated nine critical components contributing to supply chain bottlenecks due to an inability to keep up with demand, ranging from valves and actuators to switchgears and transformers. The report incorporated insights from about 30 professionals representing various parts of the satellite supply chain.
“We hear from companies that because demand is so high and capacity is not keeping up with demand,” Tomaszewski said. “That’s what’s forcing them to really make some of those hard decisions.”

According to some estimates, the next few years could mean the nearly 19,000 satellites now in LEO joined by 70,000 more. And while analysts who spoke with SpaceNews were, across the board, unwilling to speak to companies’ plans and challenges on the record, they agreed that the coming demand signal will only exacerbate already-felt bottlenecks around limited and necessary resources.

As space companies face a ramp-up in competition from Earth-based data centers for the minerals and materials they need to launch megaconstellations, experts say something’s got to give, in the form of delays, industry consolidation, material substitutions or favorable new policies. And, amid increasing global instability, certain industry shocks could be sudden and severe.
One bottleneck stems from access to the rare earth minerals that are crucial for electronic components.

Carla Filotico, partner and managing director at the European consulting firm Novaspace, told SpaceNews she’s particularly concerned about gallium nitride (GaN) and germanium, two minerals used to build high-efficiency solar cells. For common satellite materials like aluminum, the possibility of running out isn’t much of a concern, she said.

“If we assume an average of 500 kilos of mass per satellite, and we make a pure calculation of the amount of aluminum necessary, we can say that, from the primary aluminum production that is currently quite large globally, this space sector is still a niche,” Filotico said.

Space applications make up a few percent of the market demand for GaN, on the other hand, and China’s chokehold on production, at around 98%, leaves U.S. and European companies vulnerable, she said. China is also a dominant producer of germanium, for which space applications make up an even larger market share.
She added that any restrictions on gallium export could cause a shortage for the space sector that could hit at any time.
Even aluminum has become more scarce and costly amid shipping disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz caused by the U.S.-Iran conflict.

“Supply chain resilience has been a topic that has been very popular since COVID, but it’s just accelerated with more and more of these conflicts and disruptions,” said Doug Anderson, a partner at PwC’s Operations and Supply Chain Services practice who collaborated on the joint AIA report on space supply chain bottlenecks, released in March.
“The Strait of Hormuz has impacted aluminum, has impacted helium. These are things that are very important for the space supply chain,” he said.

It’s a problem with a dangling threat but no clear solution, although the last year has seen efforts to establish new mineral supply pipelines, such as a May 2025 agreement between defense prime RTX and Emirates Global Aluminum to start up gallium production in Abu Dhabi. Filotico said the worst of the resource squeeze is likely to be felt in the next five years, with the planned peak of the new constellation launch wave set to hit by 2030.
A trade disruption or geopolitical crisis that disrupts access to GaN and germanium “could certainly cause space sector shortage,” Filotico said.

And megaconstellations, due to the realities of scaling and maintenance, exacerbate the hazard of a sudden disruption to mineral supply. At one to two solar arrays per satellite, a single megaconstellation can easily require 10,000-20,000 solar panels.
“We are talking about thousands of satellites per company per year at least, because you need to replenish the satellites every four or five years, depending on the orbital height,” Filotico said.
The PwC-AIA analysis earlier this year revealed, among other things, that parts shortages are due not only to an inability to move faster and produce more, but also an unwillingness to do so.

The report described suppliers who were passing up changes to bid on space work, “citing high complexity requirements and low return on effort.” It described one case specifically in which a legacy supplier opted not to rebid on making composite overwrapped pressure vessels, needed to store high pressure gases, because the work would take about one-third of all the available engineering time while only generating “low single-digit revenue.”

At the Air Force Association’s Air Space & Cyber conference in September, Gurpartap “GP” Sandhoo, director of the Space Development Agency, said his organization continues to face supply-chain throughput and quality problems as it builds out its missile-tracking and data-transport constellations.
“We have had a demand signal, but the quality control and being able to produce things at scale has been a challenge,” Sandhoo said.

He pointed to optical communications hardware and focal-plane arrays as areas where suppliers have struggled with throughput, as well as the difficulty of manufacturing hardware that can withstand launch.

Compounding the challenges, Tomaszewski said, are a surfeit of parts pipelines with just one or two suppliers, leading to single points of failure, and new customer competition in the form of AI data centers.

Some suppliers are approaching changing buying patterns by designing parts that can scale to perform in both critical and risk-tolerant mission scenarios, Ken Stoler, a space business development lead for Arrow said on SpaceNews’ Space Minds podcast. He argued that a strong supply chain must be resilient and diverse.

The demand for data centers has notably increased even in the months since the supply chain report was released, he said, and the builders of those centers may represent a more attractive and profitable customer for suppliers of critical components than satellite constellation-makers. With switchgears and transformers specifically, the report found AI companies were “gobbling these things up at scale” and creating years-long parts backlogs.

“For a space company to come in and say, ‘Hey, we want to buy 10 of these for a new factory’ — compare that to … a big artificial intelligence company or data center company buying 10,000 of these things,” Tomaszewski said.
“The scale of it, even with the surge in space, isn’t big enough to kind of change the trajectory of where those electrical boxes are going.”

A challenge to broader efforts to ensure space companies have what they need to execute on their launch plans is a consistent and continual way to measure available resources, he said. There’s no guarantee, he added, that the nine critical components highlighted in March would still be at the top of the list today, and no simple way to find out.

“It’s been the problem with space that there hasn’t been kind of consistent awareness of where those issues are across programs, across you know national security space, civil space and commercial space,” Tomaszewski said.

That kind of data could also make it easier to enact policy interventions. For example, Tomaszewski proposes a “skip the line” authority that would allow the space industrial base to get in front of data centers and other competitors for resources.

“If we want to deliver on all these great capabilities from space and explore the solar system and beat China, you know, back to the moon, we might need to make sure that space is prioritized amongst all the other national priorities that we have,” he said.

Tomaszewski said he was encouraged by steps from the federal Office of Space Commerce to allow government and industry players to strategize over supply chain issues and discuss possible regulatory moves that could help.

“One big thing I think really still needs to get figured out is where the belly button is for fixing supply chain issues, especially at different government agencies,” he said. “Supply chain is a challenge because it is everybody’s problem, but it’s also nobody’s problem.”

Another unspoken reality, according to multiple experts, is that some megaconstellation launch plans simply won’t come to fruition, at least not as originally envisioned. Space-watchers expect to see an increase in vertical integration, in which larger companies fold parts of their supply chain into themselves. But they also anticipate industry consolidation, along with some companies dropping out of the market as they find themselves unable to achieve their objectives on their own.

“Ten, 12 years ago, when the applications were submitted with the FCC for constellations of low Earth orbit satellites, no one expected all of them to move forward, and some of them just decided not to move forward with their plans,” said Doug Stroup, president of the Satellite Industry Association. “I suspect that we’ll see some of the same thing happening with respect to the recent round of applications that have been filed.”
This article first appeared in the October 2026 issue of SpaceNews Magazine.

articles.title: NASA Names Astronaut Christina Koch Acting Deputy Chief Engineer
articles.author: Gerelle Q. Dodson

paras.en: NASA engineer and astronaut Christina Koch will serve as the agency’s acting deputy chief engineer beginning on Sunday, Nov. 1, following the retirement of Katherine Van Hooser, who will conclude more than 35 years of distinguished service to the agency on Wednesday, Oct. 21.

In her new role, Koch will help lead NASA’s engineering community, supporting technical oversight, mission readiness, and engineering excellence across the agency’s programs and projects. With this appointment, Koch will transition to management astronaut status and will no longer be eligible for future spaceflight assignments.

“Christina has seen NASA engineering from both sides of the equation: developing complex systems on the ground and trusting them with her life in space,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “After spending nearly a year living and working aboard the International Space Station and helping lead America back around the Moon on Artemis II this year, she brings an extraordinary combination of technical expertise, operational experience, and judgment to this role. I am excited to see the impact she will have across NASA as we return Americans to the lunar surface, build the Moon Base, get underway on nuclear power in space, and develop the capabilities that will ultimately take us on to Mars.”

Christina brings a unique combination of engineering expertise, operational experience, and proven leadership, both on the ground and in space. I am grateful to Katherine for her exceptional service and confident Christina will continue the tradition of technical excellence that is essential to everything we do at NASA.”

She previously spent 328 consecutive days aboard the International Space Station, setting the record for the longest single spaceflight by a woman and participating in the first all-female spacewalks.

Koch began her NASA career as an electrical engineer at the agency’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, developing scientific instruments for space missions. Before her selection as an astronaut in 2013, her experience also included scientific field engineering in Antarctica and the Arctic. She has since held leadership positions within NASA’s Astronaut Office and at the agency’s Johnson Space Center in Houston, bringing a combination of technical expertise, operational experience, and firsthand understanding of the demands of human spaceflight to her new role.

articles.title: Hurricane Simon Lurks Off the Mexican Coast

paras.en: Hurricane Simon, the latest in a long progression of tropical cyclones in the Eastern Pacific this season, passed close to the Mexican coast as a category 4 storm on October 11, 2026. Sustained winds reached 250 kilometers (155 miles) per hour as it crept north-northwest.

Simon’s eye was about 50 kilometers (30 miles) offshore, between Manzanillo and Puerto Vallarta, when the VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) on the Suomi NPP satellite acquired this image around 2:30 p.m. local time (20:30 Universal Time) on October 11.

By that time, sustained winds were about 210 kilometers (130 miles) per hour, according to the National Hurricane Center (NHC), and the storm’s inner core was brushing up against the coast. The topography of the Sierra Madre mountains appeared to temper the storm’s intensity somewhat and shrink the size of its wind field, the NHC noted. Still, the major hurricane delivered heavy rain and flooding to coastal areas, including the port city of Manzanillo, and raised the risk of mudslides in mountainous areas, according to news reports.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: In the early morning hours of October 11, satellites captured the storm’s effects extending into the upper atmosphere. This nighttime image (above), acquired with VIIRS on the NOAA-21 satellite, shows atmospheric gravity waves radiating from the hurricane. These ripples form when latent heat released near the tropical cyclone’s eyewall drives strong convection, building tall cumulonimbus clouds with updrafts that can send waves into the stratosphere and mesosphere.

But these waves are not always observable. Winds in the upper atmosphere can dissipate them before they reach the mesosphere, where they show up as ripples in airglow—faint light emitted by gases at those high altitudes. The VIIRS day-night band is sensitive to airglow but also detects reflected moonlight, which can wash it out. On the night this image was acquired, minimal illumination from the Moon helped the airglow stand out.

On the morning of October 13, forecasts of Simon’s intensity and path remained “very low confidence,” as the storm’s evolution continued to defy meteorologists’ expectations. The system may steer north and enter the Gulf of California before making landfall. Large swells causing dangerous nearshore conditions were expected along portions of the southwestern and west-central coasts of Mexico in the coming days.

articles.title: World News in Brief: West African migrant crossings, Argentina takes UK to maritime tribunal, farming in Gaza, mental health update

paras.en: World News in Brief: West African migrant crossings, Argentina takes UK to maritime tribunal, farming in Gaza, mental health update
Arrivals from Mali, Senegal, Guinea and The Gambia fell by 59 per cent in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period last year, to 4,566 people.

But the drivers of migration persist. West Africans made up a growing share of arrivals on the Mediterranean routes, accounting for 21.9 per cent on the Western route, up from 15.6 per cent, pointing to a shifting landscape.
On the Atlantic route to the Canary Islands, arrivals fell 62 per cent between 2024 and 2025, yet recorded deaths and disappearances barely changed – 1,172 compared with 1,215.
Tighter controls in Morocco, Mauritania and Senegal are pushing departures south, adding up to 750 kilometres to crossings of around 2,200 km.
“No single country can solve this alone,” said IOM Director General Amy Pope. “We need to protect migrants wherever they are.”
Argentina asks maritime tribunal to halt Falklands oil project

Argentina has asked the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (ITLOS) to order the United Kingdom to halt an offshore oil project near the Falkland Islands (Malvinas), the Hamburg-based court said on Tuesday.
Buenos Aires wants the Sea Lion development in the North Malvinas Basin stopped while an arbitration case launched by Argentina on 28 September is under way.
It also wants London to refrain from steps that could aggravate the dispute, such as granting new permits.
A hearing date will be announced shortly.
The UN lists the Falkland Islands (Malvinas) as a non-self-governing territory and has long urged both sides to negotiate.

Britain has administered them since 1833; Argentina claims sovereignty and the two countries went to war over the islands in 1982. Buenos Aires seeks to resume bilateral negotiations over the islands.
London says the islanders have the right to determine their own future and no discussion over sovereignty can occur without their consent.

Tensions have risen in recent weeks, after President Javier Milei gave London a two-week ultimatum over the project, announcing tougher measures against any companies involved in oil and gas exploration around the islands.
Gaza: increasing dangers confronting war-torn enclave’s farmers
Farmers in Gaza are facing increasing risks as they try to return to their fields.
In an update on Tuesday, the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), warned that the so-called Yellow Line of demarcation controlled by the Israeli military continues to expand into western Gaza.
This has increasingly limited access to agricultural land and prevented farmers from planting new crops.
FAO highlighted the case of 39-year-old grower Maryam, who described her small vegetable farm as a “lifeline” for her family of eight in southern Gaza.
Maryam is one of 1,700 farmers supported by FAO to purchase seeds, water and the other inputs they need to grow crops. The agency also helps herders and fishing families in Gaza
In her first season, Maryam harvested approximately three tonnes of okra.
“Farming is my life and my family’s life. It is the income source I depend on. Being able to farm again means that I am alive and that I can live with dignity with my family,” she told FAO.
WHO supports call for mental health care in the community
There’s a new call from the UN World Health Organization (WHO) to reform mental health services by developing community-based models.
According to WHO, about half of all those living in psychiatric hospitals and other institutions around the world had no choice when they were admitted.
This is despite the fact that people living with mental health conditions “can flourish in their communities when given the right support”, the agency insisted.

Mark van Ommeren, Head of WHO’s Mental Health and Substance Use Unit, said large numbers in need of services “are forced to live beyond closed doors. About half were brought in against their will, stripped of basic daily choices like what to wear, when to eat and cut off from the outside world.”
Who said on Tuesday that many countries still rely heavily on psychiatric institutions and that across the world, nearly half of all public mental health funding is spent on maintaining them.
This leaves millions of people unable to get the care they need in general hospitals or in the community.
The WHO applauded Sri Lanka for replacing its isolated mental health institutions with community-based services.
Today, the country delivers care through inpatient and outpatient units in hospitals, clinics and rehabilitation units.
“When care is characterized by coercion, rigid control, or social isolation, it risks becoming a form of confinement rather than care,” WHO stressed.

articles.title: 800 million young people face a future without jobs

paras.en: 800 million young people face a future without jobs

Approximately 800 million young people entering the labour market in developing economies over the coming years will not find jobs unless countries act, the head of the UN Development Programme (UNDP) warned on Tuesday, as the agency launched two initiatives to boost investment and employment.

“If you look at the next 15 years, there will be 1.2 billion young people graduating from school, going into the labour market,” UNDP Administrator Alexander De Croo told a press briefing in New York from Bangkok, where he is attending the World Bank Group-International Monetary Fund (IMF) Annual Meetings.
“Unfortunately, for only 400 million of these, there will be jobs. For 800 million of these, there will not be jobs.”
Mr. De Croo said the gap was driven by demographics – in many developing countries, the median age is between 18 and 25 – and that the job projections were based on the current state of technology.
“That is not going to go by itself. This is the result of policy,” he said.

Of the two initiatives, the Investment Accelerator will help governments improve investment policies and legal frameworks, build pipelines of investment-ready projects and move them from preparation to implementation.
The Jobs for Prosperity Facility will help countries identify sectors with strong job-creation potential, align skills with what employers need and tackle barriers to business investment and hiring.

Asked whether artificial intelligence (AI) was a factor, Mr. De Croo said the projections could change through active labour policies, noting that sectors such as care, agriculture and tourism would still create many jobs even as AI accelerates.
“Job creation is actually the only real sustainable way for people to grow out of poverty,” he said.

Both initiatives are backed by expanded partnerships with the World Bank Group, the European Investment Bank and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, with pilot initiatives already underway in Nepal, Yemen, Haiti, Lebanon and Ghana.
The launch comes as many developing countries face what Mr. De Croo called a “triple shock”: high energy costs, one of the most pronounced El Niño events since 1950, and very high borrowing costs.
According to a new UNDP report, No Time to Recover, the median developing country now spends 9.5 per cent of total government income on interest payments alone.
For the first time since 2010, the number of people living in multidimensional poverty – which measures not only income but also access to electricity, water, health care and education – has risen.
“Those numbers should absolutely be a wake-up call to all of us,” Mr. De Croo said.
While the global economy has proved more resilient than expected, that resilience is not shared equally, he added.
“Some countries have still quite strong economic fundamentals. Others do not have the fundamentals to withstand further shocks.”

articles.title: Yemen: Houthi siege, cholera outbreak and aid cuts put civilians in the crosshairs

paras.en: Yemen: Houthi siege, cholera outbreak and aid cuts put civilians in the crosshairs

Yemen’s southwestern city of Taiz is facing a “devastating” humanitarian crisis as escalating tensions are dramatically driving up food prices and causing shortages of supplies, the UN Spokesperson said on Tuesday.
Taiz, Yemen’s third largest city, has been a major battleground between the Iran-backed Houthis and the internationally recognised Saudi-backed Yemeni government since the start of the war in 2014.
The Houthis have besieged the city since 2015 but tightened their blockade at the start of this month when they took control of the last main road between Taiz and other government-held areas.
The development is part of a broader offensive the Houthis launched in early September to seize key territory along Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast.

Current wheat and flour supplies in Taiz could run out in less than three weeks, while food prices have reportedly risen about 50 per cent and cooking gas has become largely unavailable, the UN warns.
Petrol prices have also tripled and fuel shortages are putting water supply and health services at risk.

“We continue to urge [the parties] to…uphold their obligations under international humanitarian law and to refrain from direct attacks against civilians and civilian infrastructure and take constant care to spare both civilians and the infrastructure they use,” The UN’s Stéphane Dujarric stressed on Tuesday.
At the same time, across the country, escalating conflict and mass displacement have disrupted health services and pushed people into overcrowded shelters with inadequate access to safe water.
As a consequence, Yemen is seeing a surge in cholera – an acute and potentially fatal intestinal infection, which mostly spreads through water or food contaminated by human faeces.
The country has reported 8,034 suspected cholera cases and 27 deaths this year, with a quarter of them occurring in the last four weeks.
Since August, 200,000 people have been displaced, which the UN’s health organization WHO notes coincides with a sharp increase in cholera transmission.
Children also face serious risks from measles, with more than 22,800 suspected cases and 128 deaths reported this year.
Vaccination coverage, at an estimated 45 per cent for each of the two recommended doses, is critically low in Yemen, increasing the risk of outbreaks of vaccine-preventable diseases.
Health facilities, which are already treating thousands of people injured in the fighting, are struggling to keep up with the growing disease burden.
Approximately 500 health facilities across nine affected governorates lack partner support, the WHO found.

The agency is working with the Yemeni government to strengthen surveillance, testing and treatment, but its 90-day emergency response is critically underfunded. It needs $31 million and has received just $4.3 million, less than 14 per cent of the total.

“Without urgent funding and unimpeded access to safe water, vaccination and essential health services, outbreaks could spread rapidly among already vulnerable communities,” said WHO official Dr Annette Heinzelmann.

articles.title: Concern still for Labuschagne: What England learned from SA vs Aus first Test

paras.en: Australia vs South Africa: What England learned from first Test in Durban as Matt Renshaw inspires Australia win

Matt Renshaw nails down middle-order spot for Australia as questions remain over Marnus Labuschagne place in the side; And what about rusty-looking South Africa's struggles?' Watch the second Test in Gqeberha, live on Sky Sports Cricket from 8am, Sunday (first ball 9am)

England travel to South Africa for a three-Test series starting in December, with a home Ashes on the horizon next summer, so what can they glean from Australia's 214-run win in Durban to open their own series in South Africa?
England won't get benefit of rusty-looking Proteas

It's nearly a year since the Proteas last played Test cricket - an impressive 2-0 series win in India - while this represented their first home Test since winning the World Test Championship final against Australia at Lord's in June 2025.
They looked short of a gallop, as a result.
- Josh Hazlewood fires Australia to first-Test win over South Africa
- How Kevin Pietersen could impact England's Ashes batters
- Latest Sky Sports deals or stream with no contract on NOW

There were encouraging contributions from Aiden Markram - in particular his 237-ball, near six-hour stay at the crease in the second innings in South Africa's ultimately futile attempt to bat out for a draw - and David Bedingham, who did well with a couple of 40s at No 3.

But they weren't telling enough totals for the longer format, with South Africa guilty of throwing away numerous starts in the first innings - six players scoring at least 30 but failing to kick on - as they surrendered a 106-run deficit.

There were a couple of failures from Ryan Rickelton at the top of the order, while the captain's contribution will also be questioned as Temba Bavuma managed just four runs total across his two innings.
The question is whether this was a sign of deeper problems for the side or simply the inevitable consequence of a rusty return to Test cricket after their extended absence.

England should have their answer by the time they arrive in South Africa ahead of their first Test in Johannesburg on December 17, as the hosts have two further Tests against Australia, followed by a two-match series against Bangladesh in November to get sufficiently up to speed.
Has Renshaw solved Australia's middle-order issues?
With his first-innings, career-best 190, Matt Renshaw might just have cemented himself a middle-order spot for Australia for the foreseeable future.

The player of the match - who also chipped in with 82 in the second innings and a couple of wickets with his part-time off-spin - helped rescue Australia from 124-6 on day one when in danger of surrendering control of the contest amid familiar top-order batting failings.
Instead, Australia posted a score of 390 deep into day two and never looked back from there.
If Renshaw has indeed grabbed hold of the No 5 position, at least for the rest of the series, there are still questions to be resolved regarding the makeup of the rest of the batting line-up.

Travis Head, for example, had previously made that position his own before being bumped up to open midway through the Ashes last winter. It was a move that paid dividends at the time, as he hit three hundreds in winning causes at Perth, Adelaide and Sydney. However, he has not passed 22 in his three Test appearances since, including falling foul of a couple of soft dismissals in Durban.
Renshaw has also opened previously for Australia, so might there be a switch of the two at some point? One to revisit prior to their trip to England next summer, perhaps?
For now though, Renshaw will surely get the benefit of a run in the middle order and Australia have bigger batting issues to resolve before determining how to best use Head.
Questions remain over Labuschagne and top order
Marnus Labuschagne's wait for a 12th Test ton lives on, stretching back to July 2023.
A hundred in the warm-up match prior to the series promised much, as did his pair of 37s in this Test before failing to convert either into a score of note - let alone a century.

Averaging only 25.29 with the bat in his 24 Tests played since last topping three figures at Old Trafford in the 2023 Ashes, Labuschagne was considered incrediblly fortunate to keep his place in this Australian side but it came as a result of a lack of alternative options staking a claim.

Maddinson last played Test cricket for Australia in late 2016, averaging 6.75 across his three appearances, with his career since stalled by injury, mental health issues, and then a testicular cancer diagnosis that sidelined him for most of last year.
As a result, the 34-year-old hadn't played a first-class match since March 2025 before returning to the Test team in Durban after injuries to other batting options Cameron Green and Josh Inglis.

His first-innings 33-ball duck was an inauspicious start to his second coming in international cricket, and though he played with a great deal more freedom in the second innings, with Australia well ahead of the game by that stage - striking six fours and a couple of sixes in his 48 off 38 balls - his place in the team will continue to come under scrutiny.
Especially as Green and Inglis are now set to be back available for the second Test in Gqeberha.

To jettison Maddison after only one game back would be incredibly harsh, but Australia will be eager to get golden-boy Green, in particular, back into the team - and Renshaw has blocked his most obvious route for return at No 5.
Could he come in for Labuschagne at No 3, or Beau Webster at No 7 after he was underused as an all-rounder here? There's still much to be resolved with the look of this batting line-up.
Hazlewood and co prove they're still a force
If there was one aspect of Australia's performance that should concern England, however, it's the continued quality and depth of their bowling attack.

Josh Hazlewood's career-best Test figures of 6-49 in the second innings completed a dominant performance by the visiting seamers. Skipper Pat Cummins had led the attack first time around, taking 3-54 to help dismiss South Africa for a below-par 284 on a decent batting deck.
The evergreen talents of 38-year-old off-spinner Nathan Lyon add a further dimension, while Australia also boast Scott Boland and Michael Neser in reserve.

That depth will matter over the coming months. Australia's attack is an ageing group, and the demands of an intense Test schedule - a four-match series at home to New Zealand and five away in India - following the trip to South Africa will test their fitness and durability.
How will they be holding up by the time the Ashes comes around on June 18 with the first Test at Trent Bridge?
For the time being though, any optimistic talk of Australia's attack being past their best by then looks massively premature.
South Africa team selection a head-scratcher
South Africa's team selection for the series opener raised some questions, particularly the decision to field two specialist spinners in Durban.

Keshav Maharaj and Simon Harmer offered a left and right-arm option, but neither proved particularly potent, with just the four wickets shared between them - including only one in the first innings, to Harmer's name, allowing Australia to recover from 124-6 to post 390.

The absence of Kagiso Rabada, having failed to recover from a hamstring injury in time for this Test, perhaps forced the selectors' hand, but it left their attack looking a little lopsided and somewhat patched together.
Wiaan Mulder, for example, should not be operating with the new ball in Test cricket.
The batting all-rounder took two wickets with it on the first morning, and burgled a couple more into day two, but was pretty ineffective otherwise for his 31 overs of hard toil through the Test.

The return of Anrich Nortje was encouraging. After an extended absence from Test cricket, the fast bowler showed glimpses of the pace and aggression that made him a major asset during his first stint in the side from 2019 to 2023.
And assuming Rabada is back fit and available for the second Test in Gqeberha, his return would provide greater balance and potency to South Africa's attack.
The prospect of Rabada, Nortje and the left-arm option of Marco Jansen steaming in would represent a much sterner challenge for Australia, and England in a couple months' time.

Chris Billam-Smith might set aside his pursuit of Jai Opetaia to look at other options himself.
Billam-Smith has long wanted to box Australia's Opetaia, who is widely regarded as the best cruiserweight in the world.

But Opetaia is expected to move to heavyweight to fight former world champion Deontay Wilder on the Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua undercard before a potential bout with the outstanding cruiserweight David Benavidez next year.

articles.title: Why has Scheffler been world No 1 so long and who could replace him?

paras.en: Scottie Scheffler: Will world No 1 break more Tiger Woods records in top spot and who could be next to replace him?

When will someone eventually replace Scottie Scheffler as world No 1? Who is likely to challenge him at the top of the world rankings? And how much longer can he continue his PGA Tour dominance? We take a closer look at Scheffler's Tiger Woods-like spell as the star of men's golf
Scottie Scheffler continues to be the dominant world No 1 in men's golf, but how long will he stay top of the rankings and will he put more of Tiger Woods' records under threat?

Scheffler remains the most recent addition to the list of 25 players to have topped the Official World Golf Ranking (OWGR) since its introduction in 1986, with the American having four different spells at No 1 so far in his career.

The latest spell remains unbroken since May 2023, with Scheffler - as of October 12 - entering his 178th consecutive week as world No 1 and with a larger advantage over world No 2 Rory McIlroy than the Northern Irishman has over almost every active professional.

Scheffler is expected to only tee it up once more in 2026, at the Hero World Challenge from December 3-6 - an event he has finished first or second in four times over the last five years - although he already looks to have locked in starting the new year as No 1.
- How Scheffler enjoyed more FedExCup success on PGA Tour
- PGA Tour: Latest headlines, reports and highlights
- Get the latest Sky Sports deals or stream with no contract
How do the rankings work and why is Scheffler so far ahead?
The world rankings run over a rolling two-year cycle, with points awarded based on the strength of that tournament's field and how high a player finishes on the leaderboard.

A golfer's world ranking then comes from dividing the number of points earned by the number of tournaments someone has played during the cycle, while bonus ranking points are given to players who have won multiple events in a 52-week period.

Scheffler registered two major wins among his six worldwide titles in 2025 and already has three victories in 2026, a campaign in which his remarkable consistency has seen him post top-three finishes in half of his 20 worldwide starts.

"He's the best player in the world by a country mile," said Sky Sports' Andrew Coltart. "It's his distance control and his ability to get scoring irons pin-high basically all the time, along with an incredible level of consistency.
"Also, very importantly, I think it's his golfing IQ and his understanding of how his game is and where his game is at - that's why he's the dominant force in the game."
How has Scheffler cemented himself as No 1?

Claiming his first three PGA Tour titles in a seven-week stretch saw Scheffler take top spot for the first time in March 2022, a fortnight before his maiden major victory at The Masters, a position he held until McIlroy overtook him that October.

Scheffler enjoyed a one-week burst back at the top after his 2023 WM Phoenix Open win and another four-week run after winning The Players the following month, before Jon Rahm leapfrogged him with his second major win secured at Augusta National.
Rahm would lose top spot when Scheffler tied-second at the PGA Championship a month later, with no player since able to end his ever-increasing reign as world No 1.

"He has managed to stay at the top for so long because he has no weaknesses across his game," Sky Sports' Nick Dougherty said. "He was once a below-average putter, but he's now world class and a top-10 putter.

"The iron play is peerless - he's not just the best, he's the best by a mile when he's at his very peak. He leads birdie average and leads bogey avoidance. When you look at all of that together, there's just a reason he's better than everyone in every area."

Only Woods and Greg Norman have spent longer in their careers at world No 1 than Scheffler, who aged just 30 has already won 22 PGA Tour titles - including four majors and three legs of the career Grand Slam - and cemented his status among the greats.

Woods was world No 1 for 281 consecutive weeks from June 2005 to October 2010, breaking his own record of 264 weeks previously held from August 1999 to September 2004, with Scheffler the closest to ever seriously threaten those historic runs.

Scheffler would need to remain in top spot until October 2035 to overtake Woods' career total of 683 weeks as No 1 but only until mid-October 2028 to break the longest consecutive spell, although he has plenty of work to do to reach that milestone.

"I have absolutely no valid reason why he won't [pass 281 weeks], when you look at what he's doing right now, but the level rises around you," Dougherty added. "Whether it's Rory coming back for him again or whether he has a little bit of a slump.

"Golf is just really hard to be that good for that long. Other than Tiger Woods we've never really seen it, other than Scheffler. There's new kids on the block too and they're all hungry, so I've got a feeling someone will get to him before then."

Dame Laura Davies added: "No [he won't break the record], because of the challenging pack behind him. It won't be that he necessarily drops off that much, I just think there's way too many good players just in behind him. Over two years, it's a long time."
Will Woods or McIlroy ever return to world No 1?
Woods is currently listed as 'unranked' in the OWGR standings, having not played an official event since The Open in July 2024 and only completed four 72-hole tournaments over the last six seasons.

The 50-year-old has previously ruled out a return to full-time professional golf and is unlikely to ever return to being one of the world's best, but McIlroy has continued to be Scheffler's closest challenger to the No 1 spot.

McIlroy has been no lower than third in the world rankings since Scheffler became No 1 and has been second since last March, with the Northern Irishman winning back-to-back Masters titles over the last two seasons.

"I think McIlroy still has another stint there [at No 1] because, when he's at his absolute strength, he is definitely alongside Scheffler," Dougherty insisted. "I think he can take him on his day, he just isn't as consistent as Scottie."
Coltart added: "For McIlroy to get back to world No 1 is really tough. He's at a different stage of his life and he's attained, arguably, what he ever set out in his life to attain.

"He's older, he's got different aspirations. I don't think the fire is necessarily there that it was in his belly when he was in his early 20s. It will be very difficult for Rory to do that and I hope that he proves me wrong."
Who is likely to be Scheffler's replacement?

Matt Fitzpatrick has moved to world No 3 after winning four times in 2026, although the Zurich Classic of New Orleans did not offer world ranking points, while Players champion Cameron Young and US Open winner Wyndham Clark complete the top five.

Scheffler previously jumped from world No 15 to world No 1 in a six-week burst in 2022, highlighting that rapid rises are possible, although any of his challengers would likely require multiple more victories to be next in line for the world No 1 spot.

"If it's not Rory to go past him, it's hard to imagine who it would be among this current crop," Dougherty admitted. "It could be someone like Jackson Koivun, who is a new arrival and he's a superstar that clearly stands out already.
"It could be one of these young guns, it could even be someone we don't know yet, that's going to displace him at the top of the game."
Chris Gotterup, Sam Burns and Si Woo Kim have also made big rises up the world rankings in 2026, while Koivun and Miles Russell are others tipped to have big futures on the PGA Tour.

"There's half a dozen of them that could string together results, because that's what world No 1 is all about - consistency," Davies said. "At some point, someone will go past him. Who will that be? We'll have to wait and see.
"Watch this space, because they're all very good. He [Scheffler] is just that little bit better at the moment."
